summary: Coronado sits on a tied island — a tombolo — where a narrow sand spit called the Silver Strand connects what would otherwise be an island to the mainland, giving the city water on nearly every side: the Pacific to the west, San Diego Bay to the east, and the bay curving around the north. That geography means a roughly 32-square-mile footprint that is overwhelmingly flat, sea-level, and walkable, with unobstructed sunset views over the ocean and skyline views of downtown San Diego across the harbor. Naval Air Station North Island, occupying the northern third of the landmass, is the dominant employer and shapes the local economy around defense and federal spending — this is emphatically not a bedroom community, though the Coronado Bay Bridge funnels commuters into San Diego proper in about fifteen minutes when traffic cooperates. The affordability math is stark: a median home value near $2 million against a median household income of roughly $135,000 produces a price-to-income ratio above 14:1, meaning purchasing requires substantial wealth beyond local earnings alone, while median rent at $3,250 claims nearly 29% of that gross income. Daily life revolves around Orange Avenue's compact stretch of restaurants, independent shops, and coffee spots — genuinely walkable in a way most Southern California towns are not — and Coronado Beach, consistently ranked among the best urban beaches in the country, sits minutes from almost any front door. With average highs around 71°F year-round, roughly nine hours of daily sunshine, and lows rarely dipping below the upper fifties, the climate barely has seasons. Coronado is essentially a small, flat, military-adjacent beach town wearing a multi-million-dollar price tag — and that tension between its modest physical scale and its extraordinary cost defines everyday life there.
